paragraphs: Friend, here's what I love about this psalm. David is in a cave, running from King Saul, and he doesn't pretend it's fine. He cries out, "Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy, for in You my soul takes refuge." (Psalm 57:1) Taking refuge in God doesn't mean the trouble isn't real. It means you know exactly where to run when it is.

Notice what David does in the middle of the mess. He talks about the lions and the nets and the pits, and then he turns and says, "Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth." (Psalm 57:5) He says he will take shelter "until the danger has passed" (Psalm 57:1), and he says God "fulfills His purpose for me" (Psalm 57:2). So the danger doesn't get the last word, and God's purpose doesn't get cancelled by a cave. I spent years in a drawer thinking my story was over, so I'm telling you, hard seasons are not the end of the story!

That's why David can say, "My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast. I will sing and make music." (Psalm 57:7) His song doesn't wait for the danger to leave, because it rests on this: "Your loving devotion reaches to the heavens, and Your faithfulness to the clouds." (Psalm 57:10) So the next time you're stuck in your own cave, baker, run to God first and sing second. He's big enough to hold you, and His glory is bigger than whatever is chasing you.
